ideas.title: Sales managers paid on the team total spend their coaching on the stars. Pay them per territory and the attention shifts to the reps who need it, and performance rises
ideas.angle: Everyone argues about rep commissions. Almost nobody looks at how the manager's bonus is built, and this study says that structure decides who gets coached. When managers are paid on one team-wide number, they lean toward their star performers. When one firm switched to targets for each territory, managers moved coaching to the weaker territories, and overall performance improved most where it had been worst. For HBR, Fast Company or sales and HR trade outlets.
ideas.why_now: Online 6 days (date verified), Journal of Marketing, no coverage found. Bosses favoring their stars is a familiar complaint, and this puts data behind it.
ideas.is_it_real: Moderate. The main evidence is a quasi-experiment at one firm that changed its bonus scheme, plus one more field study, a scenario experiment with practicing sales managers, and a survey of sales leaders. Because the core data come from one company, it may not hold in other industries. The 'they moved coaching, not effort' explanation rests partly on the scenario experiment and self-reports, not on watching what managers actually did. The abstract hedges it as 'may stem from,' so the pitch should hedge it too. Performance went up after the switch, but this was not a randomized rollout.
ideas.other_peg: Year-end compensation planning: many companies set next year's sales comp plans in Q4

studies.headline: Why paying sales managers on the team total backfires — and "star bias" is the reason
studies.caveats: The core quasi-experiment and field study come from a single firm, so generalization across industries is unproven; the mechanism evidence rests partly on a scenario-based experiment and a self-report survey of sales leaders rather than observed allocation behavior.
studies.fact_check_note: ⚠️ Minor issues: Design and results match the abstract; the mechanism is stated more definitively than the abstract's hedged "may stem from" / "no evidence of an increase" wording, though the caveat partly covers this.

ideas.title: Do vaginal laser and radiofrequency treatments fix bladder leaks? A sham-controlled trial found the device added nothing and doubled side effects
ideas.angle: An evergreen page on energy-based vaginal devices sold for urgency and leaks to women in perimenopause and menopause. In a double-blind trial, radiofrequency did no better than a sham treatment when both groups also got bladder training and pelvic floor work. The device group had about twice as many adverse events. The page should explain what does have evidence and what to ask before paying out of pocket.
ideas.why_now: Med spas and gynecology practices sell these treatments for cash, and searches for them are steady. A new sham-controlled trial is the strongest kind of receipt for this question.
ideas.is_it_real: Fairly solid for its narrow question. 140 women aged 45 to 65 at two Brazilian public hospitals, randomized and double-blind with a sham procedure, followed for six months. It shows the radiofrequency adds nothing over behavioral therapy. It does NOT show behavioral therapy 'beat' the device: the digest's '$0 approach beat' headline is wrong, because both arms got behavioral therapy and there was no untreated group. Some of the improvement in both arms could be placebo or natural ups and downs. Outcomes were questionnaires and bladder diaries, so not generalizable past 65 or past six months. The online date is unverified (the PMID suggests it is months old), which is another reason this is a brief, not a pitch. The FDA's 2018 safety warning on energy-based vaginal 'rejuvenation' devices is useful background for the page.

studies.headline: A $0 approach beat a high-tech device for overactive bladder in a rigorous sham-controlled trial
studies.caveats: Participants were aged 45-65, so findings may not fully generalize to women over 70; primary outcomes were questionnaire- and diary-based; conducted at two Brazilian public hospitals; follow-up limited to six months.

ideas.title: Using AI at work cost people their boss's trust in a set of experiments, unless the company had openly encouraged it
ideas.angle: The quick take: supervisors trusted AI-assisted work less than work people did themselves, though more than plagiarized work, and rated those employees lower on performance and promotability. The one thing that erased the penalty was a stated company policy encouraging AI use. Caveat in a clause: most of the studies were lab games, not real offices.
ideas.why_now: Many workers use AI with no guidance from their employer, and whether to say so is a live question. A roundup doesn't need a peg, and this one has no honest peg for a pitch.
ideas.is_it_real: Modest. Six studies in The Leadership Quarterly. Five are incentivized economic games, and the one field study involved only academic supervisors. Promotability is the supervisor's perception, not real promotion records. The online date is unverified and at least 33 days old, so a pitch would need a peg, and there isn't a solid one. That's why it goes to roundup.

studies.headline: Your boss trusts you less when you use AI — unless the company has told you to
studies.caveats: Five of the six studies are incentivized economic games rather than real work decisions; the field study is confined to academic supervisors; downstream outcomes such as promotability are perceptions, not actual promotion records.
studies.fact_check_note: ✅ Accurate: Design (six studies, five incentivized games plus academic field study), the trust ordering (own work > LLM > plagiarism), the policy-only moderation, the downstream perceptual outcomes and the Study 6 breadth effect all match the abstract. Caveats correctly note the artificial settings and that promotability is a perception.

ideas.title: The flu-like crash after a Reclast infusion: how common it is, and whether taking ibuprofen beforehand helps
ideas.angle: An evergreen page for women starting yearly zoledronic acid (Reclast) for osteoporosis. It covers the acute-phase reaction (fever, aches, bone pain in the first days), how often it happens, and whether taking an NSAID first lowers the odds. The fear of a repeat reaction is a known reason people skip their second dose.
ideas.why_now: People search steadily for 'Reclast side effects' when an infusion is scheduled. This also fits next to the existing menopause-site brief on stopping Prolia.
ideas.is_it_real: Thin to moderate. Retrospective and single-center (one Chinese hospital), 200 patients, with propensity matching but no randomization. The reaction rate was 38% with an NSAID vs 53.2% without, about 15 points absolute (roughly 29% relative, not quite the digest's 'a third'). The benefit was mostly less pain, not less fever. The brief should rely on earlier randomized trials of pre-treatment with painkillers, which the brief room needs to find and verify, and use this study as supporting evidence. The online date is unverified and the PMID suggests about a year old, which is fine for a brief. Readers should check with their prescriber before taking an NSAID because of kidney and stomach risks.

studies.headline: A common over-the-counter painkiller taken before an osteoporosis infusion cuts the risk of a painful flu-like reaction by a third
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, retrospective, small sample (N<100 in non-NSAID group after matching)
